item.title: Basics of Nextflow
item.dc:creator: Lina Andersson
item.description:
Traditionally, you would have about one script per tool, all of which you deploy by hand, one after the other. Together, this is called a workflow or pipeline.

Manual deployment of pipelines is not always the most effective path to take in cases of: * Many steps in your analysis * Many files needing processing * Files with different sizes; one takes a minute to run, another takes an hour…

With the goal of automizing pipelines/workflows a software was made: workflow managers. What does it do? * Coordinates the deployment of the scripts in the appropriate sequence * Monitors the jobs * Handles the file transfers between scripts * Gathers the output * Handles re-execution of failed jobs for you * Can run containers -> which eliminates software installation and version conflicts

There are two workflow managers that are widely used: snakemake and nextflow.

Nextflow pipeline

In practice, a Nextflow workflow is made by joining together different processes. Each can be written in any scripting language that can be executed by the Linux platform (Bash, Perl, Ruby, Python, etc.).

Processes are executed independently and are isolated from each other, they only communicate via channels.

In Nextflow there are two kinds of channels: queue channels and value channels: * queue channel is a non-blocking unidirectional FIFO queue which connects two processes, channel factories, or operators. * value channel also called singleton channel is bound to a single value and can be read an unlimited number of times without consuming its content.

Any process can define one or more channels as an input and output.

Here is a process block that describes the picture above as part of a Nextflow pipeline:

process PROCESS_NAME{

    input:
      data z
      data y
      data x

    // directives
    container

    script:
      task1
      task2
      task3

    output:
      output x
      output y
      output z
}
  • process defines what command or script is executed
  • executor determines how that script is run in the target platform.
Note

If not otherwise specified, processes are executed on the local computer. This is useful for: * Workflow development * Testing purposes

However, real-world computational workflows a high-performance computing (HPC) or cloud platform is often required.

item.title: Pixi for environment management
item.dc:creator: Lina Andersson
item.description:
Differing software versions and dependencies break reproducibility. We solve this for command-line bioinformatics tools with Pixi environments.

Windows doesn’t really support most bioinformatics tools, or your computer might run a different version of a specific tool than mine. One way to solve this, and make research more reproducible, is through the use of environments.

In this post, I will show you how to use Pixi to create a reproducible environment for your bioinformatics tools. Since, we are working on a Linuxserver, we will use the command line to install and use Pixi.

Install Pixi

Use the following command to install Pixi on your server. This will download and install the latest version of Pixi:

wget -qO- https://pixi.sh/install.sh | sh

Next, you need to source your shell, you need to source the startup files, in Linux it’s the source ~/.bashrc file.

Create a Pixi Environment

Use the following command to create a new Pixi environment:

pixi init lina_pixi_training -c conda-forge -c bioconda

This will create a new environment called lina_pixi_training and install the necessary dependencies from the conda-forge and bioconda channels. The folder now contains a pixi toml file, which contains the environment specifications. You can edit this file to add or remove dependencies as needed. This will look something like this:

[workspace]
channels = ["conda-forge", "bioconda"] #Added channels - these are the sources we allow for our dependencies/ tools.
name = "lina_pixi_training" #The name of the environment.
platforms = ["linux-64"] #Operating system the environment is optimised for
version = "0.1.0" 

[tasks] #This is where we can define tasks - interesting, but not covered in this course.

[dependencies] #Here will be the list of tool installed within the environment (once we have added them).

In addition, the .gitignore and .gitattributes files are created automatically so that the environment can be version controlled.

Adding dependencies in Pixi.toml

Adding dependencies to the .toml file is telling Pixi to install the specified program for you. However, instead of installing it globally, it only gets installed in the environment.

To add a dependency, you can either edit the pixi.toml file directly, or use the command line. Don’t forget to cd into the environment directory first! For example, to add Quarto, you can run:

pixi add quarto

This will add Quarto to the list of dependencies in the pixi.toml file, and install it in the server environment ONLY. The pixi.toml file will now look like this:

[dependencies] 
quarto = ">=1.9.38,<2"

Once you have used the environment, or added a dependency/tool to it, you will find yet another file, called pixi.lock, which contains the exact versions of all dependencies in the environment. This file is important for reproducibility, as it allows others to recreate the exact same environment.

OBS! Do not delete the .toml or .lock files, or you will break your environment!

Running a tool with Pixi

Use Pixi to run a tool in the environment. For example, to run Quarto, you can use the following command:

pixi run quarto --help

Here, the –help flag will show you the help message for Quarto. You can replace --help with any other command or flag that you want to use with Quarto.

To use other tools, simply substitute quarto with the package you’ve added.

item.title: Quality Control using Pixi
item.dc:creator: Lina Andersson
item.description:
In any dataset involving bioinformatics, it is important to perform quality control (QC) on the raw data before proceeding with any downstream analysis. In this post, I will show you how to run QC using Pixi environments, FastQC and MultiQC.

Poor quality sequencing data can be caused by: - Sample contamination/degradation - Improper library preparation - Technical issues during sequencing

item.title: How to add a GIF
item.dc:creator: Lina Andersson
item.description:
Here, I learned how to add a GIF to a Quarto blog post.

![](duck-dance.gif)

I also learned that you can add a GIF to a Quarto blog post by using the ![]() syntax in Markdown. The GIF file should be placed in the same directory as the Quarto file or in a subdirectory, and you can reference it using the relative path. Alternatively, if you leave the path empty, Quarto will look for the GIF in the same directory as the Quarto file automatically.

Isn’t that great? It makes me wanna do aduck dance!

item.title: Publish a Quarto Blog via GitHub
item.dc:creator: Lina Andersson
item.description:
When first making a Quarto blog, it can be a bit tricky to figure out how to publish it online. In this post, I will walk you through the steps to publish your Quarto blog via GitHub Pages.

Prerequisites

  1. Make a Quarto blog project. You can do this by typing Quarto: New Project in the command palette.

This will create a new Quarto project with the necessary files and folder structure for a blog. You can customize your blog by editing the _quarto.yml file and adding your own content in the posts folder.

  1. Next, start tracking your project with Git. Make sure you are in your project directory. You can do this by opening a terminal in your project directory and typing:
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
  1. Create a new repository on GitHub and connect your local repository to it. You can do this by typing the following commands in your terminal:
git remote add origin <your-github-repo-url>
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main

Publishing in GitHub Pages

You can now publish your blog using GitHub Pages, a website hosting service. This only needs to be done once

  1. Make sure you are only rendering locally. You do this by freezing the blog to a static site by adding the following line to your _quarto.yml file:
execute:
  freeze: auto

If you have executable code in your project you’ll notice that a _freeze directory has been created. This directory stores the results of computations and should be checked in to version control. Whenever you change a .qmd file with executable code, it will automatically be re-run during your next render and the updated computations will be stored in _freeze.

  1. Next, render your blog locally by typing the following command in your terminal:
quarto render
  1. Next, you need to configure the GitHub Pages deployment for subsequent invocations. You can do this by typing the following command in your terminal:
quarto publish gh-pages
  1. Add a “workflows” directory to your .github folder and create a new file called publish.yml in it. Add the following content unchanged into the publish.yml file:
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    branches: main

name: Quarto Publish

jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Set up Quarto
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2

      - name: Render and Publish
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2
        with:
          target: gh-pages
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

This file will contain the configuration for the GitHub Actions workflow that will automatically build and deploy your blog whenever you push changes to your repository.

  1. Finally, push your changes to GitHub
